description.summary: An Appalachian folktale creature, dog- or cat-like with a long tail, that returns night after night to a hunter who cut off and ate its tail, demanding its return and ultimately killing him.
description.full: The Tailypo is a creature of North American folklore, particularly Appalachian and Southern oral tradition. In the standard tale, an isolated hunter or hermit shoots an unfamiliar animal in his cabin and severs its long tail, which he then cooks and eats. That night, and on subsequent nights, the creature returns to scratch at the cabin and call (variously) 'Tailypo, tailypo, all I want is my tailypo' or 'Who's got my tailypo?' The hunter's three hounds (often named in regional variants 'Uno, Ino, and Cumptico-Calico') drive the creature off on the first nights but are killed or scattered one by one, until on the final night the creature breaks into the cabin and kills the hunter. The Tailypo itself is described as roughly dog-sized, dark-furred, with yellow or red eyes, pointed bobcat-like ears, and a long thin tail; despite an animal appearance, it speaks plainly. Folklorists treat the Tailypo as a cautionary story about isolation, theft, and disrespect for wild creatures rather than as a cryptozoological claim.

etymology.origin: Appalachian English; the name imitates the creature's repeated call 'tailypo' for its severed tail. Spellings vary widely (Tailypo, Tailipoe, Taily-po) reflecting oral transmission.
etymology.meaning: An onomatopoeic / dialect form of 'tail' used in the creature's refrain.
etymology.first_use: Oral tradition; the tale is widely cited in 20th-century Appalachian and African-American folktale collections.

related_phenomena.name: Wampus Cat
related_phenomena.description: Other Appalachian / Southern feline cryptid of cabin-and-forest folklore

related_phenomena.name: Fearsome Critters
related_phenomena.description: North American lumberjack tall-tale tradition that overlaps Appalachian creature lore

features.description: A disproportionately long, thin tail, central to the tale; severance of the tail drives the plot
Yellow or red eyeshine in the dark
Despite an animal body, the creature speaks plain English in its repeated call

physical.morphology: Dog-sized quadruped with feline / canid features and an unnaturally long tail.

abilities.description: Calls out for the return of its tail, in dialect approximating the hunter's English
Returns night after night, escalating from scratching at the walls to entering the cabin
Approaches the cabin in darkness and kills the hounds one by one

patterns: Returns repeatedly to the place where its tail was taken
Confronts the hunter directly on the final visit

range.description: Folktale concentrated in the Appalachian region and the broader American South. The tale also appears, with variations, in African-American Southern oral tradition and in 20th-century children's-literature retellings.

first_recorded.source: Oral tradition; collected by 20th-century Appalachian and Southern folklorists

origins.cultural_roots: Appalachian English-speaking folk tradition, with significant overlap with African-American Southern oral storytelling.
origins.earliest_accounts: The tale circulates orally before its earliest published collections in the 20th century.
origins.folklore_connections: Connected to the broader Southern 'haint' tradition and to fearsome-critter and Appalachian cabin-monster tales.

timeline.event: Joanna Galdone publishes the picture-book retelling 'The Tailypo: A Ghost Story' (illustrated by Paul Galdone)
timeline.significance: Introduces the tale to a wide American children's-literature audience and stabilizes a canonical version
timeline.source: Galdone, J. (1977), The Tailypo: A Ghost Story (Clarion Books)

history.modern_era: The Tailypo continues to circulate as a campfire and ghost story across the American South, in middle-school folklore curricula, and in regional storytelling festivals. It is also routinely featured in twenty-first-century horror-podcast retellings.

documentary.name: The Tailypo: A Ghost Story
documentary.description: Picture-book retelling of the Tailypo tale by Joanna Galdone, illustrated by Paul Galdone, that became a canonical 20th-century version.
documentary.analysis: Primary modern textual witness of the tale; widely used in U.S. school folklore units.

skeptical.name: Cautionary folklore
skeptical.description: Folklorists treat the Tailypo as a moral tale about taking what is not yours and disrespecting wild creatures, rather than as a report of an actual animal.
evidence_cited: Multiple regional variants with shared moral arc

stories: Variant in which the hounds Uno, Ino, and Cumptico-Calico are named
folklore.beliefs: The Tailypo is not generally treated as a real animal, but as a frightening cautionary tale used in cabin and campfire storytelling, in which violation of an unfamiliar creature's body brings disproportionate retribution.

literature: The Tailypo: A Ghost Story — Joanna Galdone, illus. Paul Galdone (Clarion Books, 1977)
film_tv: Tales from the Cryptkeeper and other anthology programs (occasional Tailypo-derived episodes)
other: Common entry in regional storytelling festivals across the American South

research.ongoing_studies: Tailypo continues to appear in academic folklore studies of Appalachian oral tradition, but no organized research effort treats it as a cryptozoological subject.
